title: Privilege activation lifecycle and evidence export guidelines
content:
Purpose:

This doc defines the privilege activation lifecycle (how temporary elevated permissions are requested, approved, activated, recorded, and expired), and provides practical guidance for exporting the resulting evidence to SIEM/audit pipelines across Redwood’s three hosting environments (hosted API, Dedicated, Private). It focuses on RBAC v2 constructs, audit schema additions to support evidence automation, and concrete policy snippets for environment-specific controls.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to RBAC v2 role model (roles, role-assignments, constraints, activation windows, just-in-time (JIT) elevation).
- Covers telemetry and evidence artifacts required for security reviews and audits, and mappings to SIEM fields.
- Does not replace formal change-control for high-risk infra changes — it augments access controls with automated evidence.

Why this matters (short):
- Engineers need predictable, low-friction temporary elevation for operational work; auditors need immutable, queryable evidence tied to decisions.
- A consistent lifecycle and export schema lets SRE/IR teams run fast while meeting compliance obligations.

Privilege activation lifecycle (high level):
1) Request: user initiates elevation via UI/CLI/Slack workflow. Request includes scope: role, target resource scope (e.g., tenant-id, cluster, model-id), justification, and TTL request.
2) Pre-checks: automation validates eligibility (group membership, last activity, prior approvals, cooldowns).
3) Approval: could be automated (policy-based), delegated (on-call), or manual via an approver. Approval metadata captured (approver id, method, time).
4) Activation: system issues short-lived credentials or a session token scoped to the requested role and resource. Activation record created (activation-id, requester, approver, start/end time, token id).
5) Usage telemetry: all privileged actions are tagged with activation-id and recorded in audit events (token usage, API calls, CLI commands).
6) Expiry & remediation: token auto-expires at TTL; post-activation review (if flagged) attaches results to activation evidence.

RBAC v2 fields required to support the lifecycle (recommended additions):
- role: {role_id, name, permanent:boolean, allowed_environments:[hosted,dedicated,private], max_ttl_minutes}  (store as role metadata)
- activation: {activation_id, requester_id, approver_id, role_id, resource_scope, approved_at, activated_at, expires_at, reason, policy_evidence_ids}
- eligibility_record: {user_id, groups_snapshot, last_password_change, mfa_present} (for pre-check snapshot)

Audit log schema notes (augment existing schema):
Add the following top-level fields to every audit event that can be produced under an active elevation: 
- activation_id (string) - correlates events to the privilege activation lifecycle
- elevated_role (string) - the role name/ID in effect for this action
- activation_origin (enum: portal, cli, slack, api)
- approver_id (string|null) - populated when approval required for activation
- activation_ttl_minutes (int)
- justification_text (string|null) - short reason recorded at request time
- pre_check_pass (bool) - whether automated eligibility checks passed
- evidence_refs (list<string>) - pointers to stored artifacts (signed JSON blobs, zip ids)

These fields must be preserved through any SIEM ingestion transformation. For hosted environment we recommend adding a flattened field set to CloudTrail/ingest stream; for dedicated/private, include the same fields in the local audit forwarder contract.

SIEM export mapping (recommended canonical mapping):
- event_time -> @timestamp
- user_id -> user.name
- activation_id -> event.context.activation_id
- elevated_role -> event.context.role
- approver_id -> event.context.approver
- activation_origin -> event.context.origin
- justification_text -> event.context.reason
- evidence_refs -> event.context.evidence_refs (array of strings)

Note: For large-scale exports, include both event-level and activation-level indices to allow queries like "all events for activation X" and "all activations approved by user Y in period Z" without heavy joins.

Environment-specific guidance:
1) Hosted API (multi-tenant, Redwood-managed):
- Principle: minimize permanent privileges. Prefer JIT activations mediated by Redwood console or API gateway.
- Policy: no permanent write roles for customer-facing support on production clusters; all support personnel must use activation flow with minimum TTL of 15 minutes, maximum 8 hours (configurable per severity).
- Evidence store: activation evidence (signed activation JSON + approver signature) is persisted in Redwood S3 with object lifecycle 7 years (encrypted at rest). SIEM ingest uses an internal event-forwarder that adds activation metadata before export.
- Export contract: every hosted audit event must include activation_id and evidence_refs. SIEM team should map event.context.* fields as per canonical mapping.

2) Dedicated (customer-dedicated GPU pools):
- Principle: customer must approve policy baseline; Redwood suggests default JIT enablement with centralized logging to customer SIEM or Redwood-managed SIEM if contracted.
- Policy snippet: for Dedicated, allow organization-admins to define role whitelists and TTL caps. Default enforcement: require two-step approval for high-scope activations (e.g., cluster-scope).
- Evidence store: allow option to mirror activation evidence to customer S3 or to Redwood evidence bucket with customer-specific encryption key.
- Export contract: provide a configurable forwarder (syslog/HTTPS) that carries activation_id and evidence_refs as structured fields. Avoid stripping activation metadata.

3) Private (VPC/on-prem):
- Principle: many customers will have stricter audit pipelines — Redwood must provide a minimal local contract and tooling to emit activation-linked events.
- Policy: provide a deployable appliance or agent that enforces activation lifecycle locally and writes signed evidence artifacts to the customer’s audit store.
- Evidence store: local object store or HSM-backed artifact signing; customer is responsible for retention.
- Export contract: recommend local SIEM mappings match canonical mapping; provide translation scripts and validation tests.

Evidence automation and retention recommendations:
- Evidence artifact: signed JSON bundle containing activation metadata, pre-check snapshot, approver signature, and activation_hash. Store as gzipped JSON.
- Naming convention: evidence/<env>/<year>/<month>/<activation_id>.json.gz.
- Retention: hosted default 7 years; dedicated default 3 years (customer override); private: customer-managed.
- Integrity: sign each artifact with a rotating key (KMS/HSM); publish daily key fingerprints to the audit bucket for verifiers.

Operational playbooks (quick):
- On suspicious privilege usage (automated rule): 1) flag activation as "post-review"; 2) snapshot state (running tasks, jobs launched); 3) escalate to on-call and create incident with activation_id attached; 4) attach evidence bundle to incident.
- On failed pre-check bypass (rare): revoke activation, mark as "failed_precheck" and route to security review.

Policy snippet examples (illustrative, adapt per env):
- JIT role enforcement pseudo-policy: "allow_activation_if (user.in_group('infra-oncall') AND not user.has_active_activation(role) AND requested_ttl <= role.max_ttl_minutes)"
- Approval delegation policy: "if role.scope == 'cluster' then require approver in group 'infra-leads' OR two independent approvals"

Queries auditors will ask and how to answer them quickly:
- "Show all activations for user X in last 90 days": query activations index by requester_id and date range -> return activation_ids + evidence_refs.
- "Show events for activation Y": query event index where event.context.activation_id == Y.
- "Show approver chain for high-scope activations": activation record includes approver_id(s) and approval method; evidence bundle contains approver signature.

Implementation checklist (MVP):
- [ ] Add activation schema fields to RBAC datastore and event schema.
- [ ] Ensure all privileged-action producers attach activation_id to emitted events.
- [ ] Implement evidence artifact generator and signer.
- [ ] Implement S3 evidence layout and access controls (hosted).
- [ ] Build SIEM forwarder mapping activation fields to canonical mapping.
- [ ] Provide deployment templates for Dedicated/Private forwarders.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- TTL defaults by role for different environments (suggestion: hosted: 4h default, dedicated: 8h default, private: customer-defined).
- Approval model for cross-tenant support actions in Dedicated when customer wants Redwood assistance.
- Query performance targets for activation-event correlation index (suggest starting SLA: 2s for single activation lookups).

Appendix: example activation evidence (human-readable summary):
Activation ID: act_20251103_9f3a
Requester: mliu@redwood.ai
Role: support/production-readwrite (JIT)
Approved by: asg_admin@customer.com (manual)
Requested TTL: 180 minutes
Activated at: 2025-11-03T14:11:22Z
Expires at: 2025-11-03T17:11:22Z
Pre-checks: group_membership:pass, mfa:pass, cooldown:pass
Evidence refs: [s3://redwood-evidence/hosted/2025/11/act_20251103_9f3a.json.gz]

Notes: this doc is intentionally implementation-focused. Pull requests adding activation fields to event producers should reference the linked artifacts above and add unit tests asserting activation_id propagation.

If you are reviewing: please comment with environment-specific constraints or operational concerns.
